name: Differentiated Materials
title: Differentiated Materials
answer: Differentiated materials is the practice of using AI to turn one lesson into several versions, such as a worksheet or reading passage written for students who need more support, for students at grade level, and for students ready for a challenge. It matters because teachers regularly need the same lesson at more than one level, and AI can draft those versions quickly while the teacher makes sure every version still teaches the same core content.

sections.body: Teachers often need one lesson to serve students working at different levels, and building separate versions by hand takes time. AI tools can produce three versions of a worksheet or reading passage in short order, one with more support, one at grade level, and one that stretches students who are ready. The same approach extends to other planning materials, including rubrics drafted from an assignment description, quizzes and exit tickets generated from the teacher's own lesson text, slide decks, video quizzes, and checks on whether a text's reading level suits a class. The problem it solves is preparation time, not judgement: the teacher still confirms that each version carries the same core content and that every generated item is accurate and clear.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not sort this practice by grade band, so it reads as guidance for any teacher preparing a lesson. A teacher can ask a tool such as MagicSchool to produce support, grade level and challenge versions of a worksheet or reading passage, then compare them to confirm they teach the same core content. For rubrics, AI can draft performance levels and descriptions from the assignment, after which the teacher revises them to match their own expectations and tries them against a few samples of student work. Quizzes and exit tickets work best when the teacher supplies the lesson text and asks for questions, then checks each one for accuracy and clarity before delivering it through Google Forms. Planning tools also cover slide decks through Canva for Education or Google Slides, video quizzes built by embedding a video in Google Forms with questions along the way, and readability checks that the teacher confirms by reading the text.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no evidence label, study, figure or finding for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. What it offers instead are practical rules of thumb drawn from classroom use: questions taken from a teacher's own materials are described as more reliable than questions a tool invents, and a rubric that has never been tested against real student work is said to often need adjustment. These are working cautions rather than measured results, and no comparison, sample or trial is cited to support them. Readers should treat the guidance as accumulated practice from teachers and tool users, not as a demonstrated outcome.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The decisions stay with the teacher at every step. The teacher checks that each differentiated version teaches the same core content, revises any drafted rubric to match their own expectations, and tests that rubric on samples of student work before relying on it. Every generated quiz or exit ticket question is checked for accuracy and clarity, and a readability check is confirmed by the teacher reading the text themselves. The text also warns that questions invented by a tool are less reliable than questions drawn from the teacher's own materials, which keeps the source material and the final judgement on the human side of the work.
